claims.claim: Marketing analytics is the practice of measuring and analyzing marketing data to understand what is working and to inform decisions; the American Marketing Association maintains marketing analytics as a recognized practice area with training and certifications.
Marketing metrics are measurable, quantifiable values that marketers track to assess marketing performance.
Reach counts the number of different (unique) people exposed to content, while impressions count every time the content was displayed, including repeats.
Engagement counts audience actions on content, such as likes, shares, retweets, and comments.
Clicks measure how many people clicked an ad or link; the click-through rate is the percentage of people who see an ad and click on it.
Conversion rate is the percentage of an audience that completes a desired action, calculated as the number of conversions divided by the audience size, times 100.
A marketing dashboard gathers the metrics a team has selected to track into a single view, updated regularly, giving a quick overview of progress toward goals.
Metrics record what happened but not why: an ad view or a click does not indicate intent to purchase, and there is no way to tell from the number whether the ad persuaded anyone or changed behavior.
A/B testing compares two versions of a page, email, or ad by showing each to a random slice of the audience and comparing which performs better.

Marketing analytics is ongoing measurement of marketing performance, whereas market research is a designed study that answers a specific question at a point in time; the two are related but distinct activities.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reach and impressions are defined slightly differently across platforms and tools (some platforms count repeat views within reach, others report reach as a display count).
positions: textbook definition used in this lesson: reach = unique people, impressions = total displays
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard textbook definitions (OpenStax/HubSpot) and notes that a number only makes sense when the definition is known, which is itself one of the honest limits taught.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Marketing analytics and market research overlap in practice (research projects also analyze data, and some sources treat research as a phase within analytics).
positions: this curriculum separates them: analytics = ongoing measurement; research = designed one-time studies
some industry sources use the terms loosely
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson draws the line using the two OpenStax sections (2.4 ongoing metrics; 6.1 research as a designed study) and points to the sibling market-research lesson for the research side.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing 2.4: Marketing Plan Progress Using Metrics
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20260608152121). Supports: marketing metrics defined as measurable, quantifiable values marketers aim to achieve within a specified period; KPIs tied to objectives with targets and time frames; real-time marketing dashboards providing instant visibility of selected metrics as a quick overview of standing and progress toward goals; and the honest limit that 'metrics tell us what is happening at any point in time without context as to why.' Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing 6.1: Marketing Research and Big Data
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Internet Archive capture. Supports: marketing research as the way marketers listen and assess the needs of the market, and managers needing marketing information to make data-driven decisions rather than assumptions. Used only to draw the analytics-versus-research boundary (research = designed study answering a specific question; the market-research lesson is a sibling topic). Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing 14.3: The Use of Metrics to Measure Advertising Campaign Effectiveness
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20260608152121). Supports: KPIs as indicators that measure how a campaign achieves goals; impressions as the number of times an ad appears (formula: rating x target population x number of ads run); conversion rate = number of converts / audience size x 100, with a worked 2.0% example; the marketing-dashboard section; and the honest limits of impressions ('an ad view does not indicate an intent to purchase... no way of knowing whether the ad was persuasive or changed behavior'). Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing 16.3: Metrics Used to Evaluate the Success of Online Marketing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook. Read via Internet Archive capture (web.archive.org/web/20260608152121). Supports: online marketing metrics as quantitative performance measures; website traffic and traffic by source; conversions (turning a visitor into a customer); social engagement measured by likes, shares, retweets, and comments; impressions defined as when users see the ad; click-through rate as the percentage of people who click on an ad; the marketing-dashboard heading. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Marketing Analytics (AMA topic archive)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A professional body. Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22 (ama.org blocks direct fetching of many pages; this archive page rendered). Supports: marketing analytics is a recognized practice area within marketing — the AMA maintains a topic hub with training, certifications, and events, and frames analytics around answering what marketing contributed and presenting results in plain language. Site terms prohibit reproduction; only the field-level claim is used, restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: A/B Testing (Optimization Glossary)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B/C vendor education. Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: A/B testing (also called split testing) as a methodology for comparing two versions of a webpage or app to determine which performs better, by showing the two variants to users at random and comparing results. Used for the one-line general idea only.

sourceRecords.title: Social Media Impressions vs. Reach
sourceRecords.notes: Tier C reputable secondary (corroborated by OpenStax and standard textbook usage). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: reach defined as who sees content — the total number of people who see a post — and the reach-versus-impressions distinction. Used only for the unique-people reading of reach.

sourceRecords.title: Marketing Analytics: A Beginner's Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Tier C reputable secondary (corroborated by OpenStax). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: marketing analytics tracks how prospects and leads interact with marketing initiatives and channels over time; dashboards pull data from across channels (email, ads, social) into one view; attribution of marketing activities to revenue. No industry statistics from the article were used.
